claims.text: The proposed alloy has an equiatomic FeCoNiCr composition.
Homogenized equiatomic FeCoNiCr is a single-phase fcc alloy free of secondary phases.
Homogenization at 1200°C will ensure chemical uniformity in equiatomic FeCoNiCr.
Aging FeCoNiCr at 600°C for 12 hours will form coherent nanoscale Cr-rich precipitates in the fcc matrix.
The Cr-rich precipitates will be antiferromagnetic or weakly ferromagnetic.
The Cr-rich precipitates will exchange-couple with the surrounding soft-ferromagnetic matrix.
Exchange coupling between the precipitates and matrix will produce an exchange-bias effect.
The proposed exchange-bias effect will increase domain-wall pinning and thereby increase coercivity.
Precipitation will affect saturation magnetization only modestly.
Optimized aging could produce coercivity about twice that of the earlier FeCoNiPt and FeCoNiPd derivatives.
The aged FeCoNiCr alloy will maintain high saturation magnetization.
The earlier FeCoNiPt and FeCoNiPd derivatives have low coercivity and exhibit soft ferromagnetism.
The magnitude of the coercivity change depends on precipitate characteristics such as volume fraction, size, distribution, coherency, and lattice misfit.
Excessive precipitate growth or loss of coherency may prevent the desired coercivity enhancement.
The cited literature supports an exchange-coupling mechanism for increasing coercivity through coherent nanoscale precipitates.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that coherent precipitates will pin domain walls effectively and substantially raise coercivity, whereas the cited introduction says high coherency creates negligible distortion fields and only modest domain-wall pinning, and the cited results say precipitate pinning is insignificant compared with boundary pinning.

The hypothesis predicts roughly doubled coercivity, while the cited same-topic study on a different CoFeNiTaAl system reports that coherent nanoprecipitates increased coercivity only marginally and retained coercivity below about 11 Oe.
